analysis.investment_thesis: Cemindia Projects (formerly ITD Cementation) has delivered stunning operational improvement — revenue tripled from ₹2,728 Cr to ₹9,097 Cr in 4 years, and ROCE of 27.6% is genuinely exceptional for Indian construction. However, the recent change of control to an opaque entity (Renew Exim DMCC) combined with a glaring FCF/Net Income ratio of just 8% (₹30 Cr FCF vs ₹373 Cr profit) raises serious questions about earnings quality and the future alignment of capital allocation.
key_strengths: ROCE of 27.6% and ROE of 21.8% are outstanding for a civil engineering firm — suggests specialised niche capabilities in marine structures, TBM tunnelling, and foundation engineering that command better pricing than generic construction
Revenue growth of ~3x in 4 years riding India's infrastructure capex supercycle, with net profit compounding from ₹16 Cr (FY21) to ₹373 Cr (FY25) — an extraordinary turnaround in earnings power
Conservative balance sheet with Debt/Equity of 0.48 and reasonable cash buffers (₹358 Cr) provides margin of safety against project delays or working capital shocks
key_risks: FCF of only ₹30 Cr against net profit of ₹373 Cr in FY25 — a FCF/NI conversion of ~8% — is a major red flag; either working capital absorption is structural or earnings quality is questionable
Project-based construction has no recurring revenue moat: every new contract must be won competitively, execution risk is high, and government payment delays can devastate cash flow
Heavy dependence on government/PSU clients (infrastructure ministries, ports) means order book and revenue are exposed to election cycles and fiscal policy shifts
red_flags: Ownership change to Renew Exim DMCC (August 2025) is recent and highly opaque — an unknown UAE-based entity acquiring control of a listed Indian EPC company demands serious due diligence on intent and capital allocation philosophy
Operating cash flow collapsed from ₹704 Cr (FY24) to ₹203 Cr (FY25) even as net profit rose from ₹274 Cr to ₹373 Cr — growing working capital absorption and receivables warrant investigation
Forward P/B of 5.44x is expensive for a construction company with no durable IP or brand; a single large project loss or NPA cycle could rapidly erode book value
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Cemindia possesses genuine specialised capabilities — maritime structures, TBM tunnelling, diaphragm walling — that are difficult to replicate quickly and command above-average margins. The ROCE of 27.6% over this period is not what you see in commodity civil contractors; it suggests real technical differentiation. The revenue compound from FY21 to FY25 (₹2,728 Cr to ₹9,097 Cr) reflects both India's infrastructure boom and the company winning a larger share of complex, high-value contracts. These are genuinely good signs.

However, the FCF story is deeply troubling. In a construction business where profits should progressively convert to cash as projects are completed, the ₹30 Cr FCF in FY25 against ₹373 Cr in reported profit suggests either aggressive revenue recognition, receivables ballooning, or retention money piling up. The Renew Exim DMCC ownership change is a total wildcard — I don't invest in businesses when I can't assess the values and intentions of the controlling owners. That alone warrants a 'monitor, don't commit' stance.
